messages.body_plain:
In general we don't answer questions about how to solve specific problems (of course other group members are free to do so). But let me sketch how I would go about this one, as there is an interest in how to use RHadoop for CPU bound work. First question is whether we can load one matrix in main memory? The answer should be yes by a good margin. Then let's say you have M (or the smaller of the two)  in memory and N in a hadoop file. The function cor operates on the columns, so you need to transpose both matrices.

Mt = t(M)

out = mapreduce(N, map = function(k,v) cor(Mt, t(v)))

you may want to reduce the default value for keyval.length (in rmr.options) to avoid time outs.

Antonio

Time outs are necessary, by setting them so high you are eliminating fault tolerance. You need to get your job to output something at regular intervals, like a status message if not actual output. You can call the function status to achieve that. L

> but the problem is that it runs much slower than just run in one computer. It run in R(one computer) need 20 minutes, in Rhadoop (1 namenode and 4 datanodes) need more than 40 minutes.

Comparison between in memory, sequential programs and Hadoop programs is not as straightforward as N nodes implies 1/N time. Hadoop was designed for scalability first with efficiency taking second place. That said, since your job seems to be CPU bound and decomposable into independent units (you said it's a map only job) this performance result is surprising. I don't know what the differences are in detail between the two programs being compared, nor I know if the hardware configurations involved, so it's hard for me to tell. If the map function is essentially the same as the sequential program and the hardware is comparable, then you need to use the profiler to figure out were the time is going.

> Even I set the map tasks number is 8 and see the Num Tasks is 8 in 50030, but I think it's just run to 3 tasks, I mean the real data just assign to these 3 tasks. Because the other 5 tasks is finished so quickly less than 10 seconds, and the other 3 tasks need more than 40 minutes.

Setting keyval.length to a smaller number would probably solve your time out issues but not the number of mappers issue.

> My mapfunction don't have reduce(NULL).

A map function can't have a reduce. You probably meant your mapreduce call has the reduce argument set to NULL. Using the appropriate language will go a long way in resolving your issue, as would providing a reproducible test case.

messages.body_plain:
I am currently experimenting with parallel file reads from hdfs using rhdfs, doMC, and foreach. For reasons beyond my control, rmr is not currently an option for me, so I am pulling data from hdfs directly for analysis, but I'd like to read in the files in a parallel fashion. I have tested my approach to parallel reads against local files, but when I switch to reading in data from hdfs, the process hangs indefinitely.

Example code:

require(rhdfs)
require(doMC)
require(foreach)
registerDoMC()
getDoParWorkers()

# returns 4

hdfs.path = "/user/data/2013_316/{part-00000,part-00001}"
hdfs.init()
files = hdfs.ls <http://hdfs.ls>(hdfs.path)
localFiles=data.frame(list.files("inst/extdata/", pattern="*.txt"))
colnames(localFiles) <- c("file")

Works:
test <- foreach (i=1:1) %dopar% {
  hdfs.read.text.file(files$file[i])
}

or

test <- foreach (i=1:2, .combine=rbind) %dopar% {
  read.table(file.path(getwd(), "inst", "extdata", localFiles$file[i])
             ,stringsAsFactors=FALSE,
             sep='^',
             col.names=schema$name,
             colClasses=schema$coltype,
             na.strings="",
             quote="",
             comment.char="")
}

Doesn't Work:
test <- foreach (i=1:2) %dopar% {
  hdfs.read.text.file(files$file[i])
}

I assume something must be at issue with the connection to hdfs, but as I am new to rhdfs, doMC, and foreach and fairly new to R as well, it could just as easily be something obvious I am doing wrong. I'm hoping someone can shed some light here.

I figured I'd get that question. That is why I mentioned that rmr is not an option for me just now, and it's unclear when it might be. As you know, convincing admins to allow R to be installed on nodes in a production cluster is not always the simplest thing. In the meantime, there are things we as engineers can do to get data in the hands of our R users. For instance, in my case, I have implemented the vast majority of work in traditional map reduce jobs, which will scale just fine :). The output of these jobs are prepared (cleansed, aggregated, and partitioned) data sets that are appropriate for the particular analytical needs of our R users, and small enough to fit into memory easily. Results are located on hdfs, a location chosen because it is available to not just R via rhdfs, but also hive and other map reduce jobs that make use of them. So as you can see, my desire here is to use rhdfs to eliminate both a need for secondary R specific storage and an annoying R specific ETL step. I'm trying parallelization out simply because I want to be able to load data into R from hdfs faster than in a comparatively slow serial fashion.

Would it be better if I could offer R users a direct access to detail data to run map reduce from within R? Sure, and that is despite the fact that 60% or more of work involved in analyzing large data sets often involves pre-analysis data preparation, which is not in the traditional R users' wheelhouse, and reduces their capacity to focus on real analysis. Regardless, even prepared data sets are "big data" now, and tools like rmr are definitely the future, but totally not relevant to my current use case.

Do let me know if you or your colleagues decide to look into the original issue posted. I'd appreciate any insight.

I don't know of any product where a duplicate installation is not an error. I don't think rmr2 is the exception. One installation is complete when several items have been installed on each node. That's one installation, not two or three. R-studio is neither dependent on nor necessary for rmr2. Let's  leave it out for clarity's sake.

I am more than a little uneasy about your use of the word "attack", so I will assume a typo and replace it with the word "attach" which I will replace with a more commonly used "connect". The answer is, yes, just install hadoop on the linux box so that it can connect with the cluster. The linux box doesn't have to be a name node, data node or have any role in the cluster, but still has to have hadoop installed, and will take only the duty of a client. rmr only communicates with a local hadoop installation. You can find information on this type of configuration in the general Hadoop literature.

messages.body_plain:
Well, there is installing packages on each node and there is installing rmr2 as a whole. I wish I had two separate words. To install rmr2 to a properly working state, rmr2 as an overall system, you need to install R and a number of packages on each node, in the sense of running R CMD INSTALL or equivalent. One of those packages is called rmr2 as well.  But installing rmr2 the package on a single machine doesn't complete the larger installation procedure, that sequence of steps that allows you to use rmr2. It may appear that there is a package called rmr2 installed on this or that node, but unless every node has R, rmr2 and dependencies you won't be in a working state. This requirement is common to rmr2 and plyrmr, but different from rhdfs and rhbase that can be installed on a single node and work. I wish we had an "install on cluster" command. Until then we need to make do with available tools and concepts.

Antonio

messages.subject: capture mapreduce stdout
messages.body_plain:
Story Background:

    * We are submitting R scripts through Rserve service to RHadoop
    * These scripts are run on Hadoop by means of RHadoop
    * The execution of a script will result into several Hadoop jobs
    * Several concurrent executions of scripts can occur

We have the following High Level requirements:

   1. We like to have some kind of estimated progress of the execution of an R script on Hadoop.
      For this we need to relate the execution of an R script to its Hadoop job IDs so that we can use this to query the jobtracker about the progress.
   2. Further we would like to be able to stop one already submitted R script so that all tasks in Hadoop are also stopped.

    In the moment it is only possible to stop and restart the Rserve service which will cancel all R script executions and will keep the Hadoop jobs alive.
    We like to cancel specific R script executions so we also need some kind of Hadoop job ID here to stop also all related Hadoop jobs.

    Parsing Hadoop log file could be a solution but as we can have several jobs, this will not work. Another option is to have a log file per job, I don't know how to get this. As an approach I tried to capture stdout but sink() and capture.output() don't work, I think this is related to mapreduce streaming, but I'm not sure.

    Has rmr an option to log the output of mapreduce()? I haven't found it.

    Any other solutions or hints available for these requirements?

    (We use rmr 2.2.2 on Centos, real cluster)

Thank you in advance.
 Jorge

I tried this before and gave up. The console output can be captured in R (see last few lines of function rmr2:::rmr.stream, when option verbose is FALSE it is actually captured) but becomes available only when the system call returns, that is the job is done. That's by definition too late to kill the job. Antonio

It appears it's a network problem, it manifests itself after the map phase but before the reduce phase because nodes are trying to communicate with each other. You may want to run a test mapreduce job independent of rmr2, like one of the examples that are distributed with Hadoop. The other thing is that you may want to try to ping each node from each one and make sure that they all can resolve all names. In general this looks like a hadoop problem, by just googling the error message I found several threads covering the issue. I hope this helps.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: tutorial of the RHadoop?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Felipe,

The four packages provide different functionalities.  You might want to get started with just rhdfs to read from and write to HDFS from within R.

The basic process is:
1) Install a Hadoop cluster.
2) Configure a client machine to be able to connect to the Hadoop cluster.  i.e. you should be able to run `hdfs dfs -ls`.
3) Install R  on a client machine.
4) Tell R where to find Hadoop and Hadoop streaming
    export HADOOP_HOME=/path/to/hadoop/home
    export HADOOP_STREAMING=/path/to/hadoop-streaming-version.jar
5) Configure R to use Java.
R CMD javareconf
6) Install rJava
R --no-save <<EOT
  install.packages( pkgs="rJava",
                    dependencies=TRUE,
                    repos="http://www.rforge.net" )
EOT
7) Install rhdfs
R CMD INSTALL /path/to/rhdfs_version.tar.gz

I hope this helps.

-Carlos

On Sun, Dec 22, 2013 at 11:38 AM, Risto Saari <rist...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Good points, agreed. I read this https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/plyrmr and other pages, and if i understood correctly some of the r functions are implement in rhadoop. I have used aws mr and 10 ec2 instances with good success.
>
> Whats still a challenge if i have big vector and using something like r dist function i will have out if memory. I could not find if dist is implemented in rhadoop.

Unfortunately it isn't. If I understand correctly, you have an nxm matrix and you want to compute the euclidean or other distance beteen all pairs of rows of the matrix, which will result in a nxn matrix after executing some n^2 m multiplications. The nxm matrix can fit in memory but the nxn can not. I think a very similar problem is tackled in the kmeans example. There is a matrix of points and a matrix of centers and what is desired is computing all the distances between one point and one center. For you it just happens that the set of points and the set of centers is the same. So a program could look like

M #input matrix

mapreduce(scatter(to.dfs(M)), map  = function(k,v) distxy(M,v))

Where scatter is a utility to break down a data set into smaller parts, that helps with achieving a higher level of parallelism on smaller data sets. distxy is like diist but with two arguments. It's implemented as part of the kmeans example where it is called dist.fun. As usual with small data, large compute problems you will have to work a bit to make Hadoop do the right thing as far as number of map tasks and some such: Hadoop is designed for big  data application but has been pushed into either directions, just keep in mind that it's a bit more advanced stuff and defaults may not serve you very well. The above program is a sketch, I've never run it and its final from may depend on what you are going to do it afterward.

> I am looking scale out when using r and rhadoop. Rapidminer had some hadoop specific stuf, but I think it did not have great success.
>
> If memory begans a problem in r is there a clever way to workaround it?

This is more a RHadoop discussion group then a general scalability or big data one, so I am afraid we would veer off topic nor you would get the best answers by seeking this kind of information here. The range of solutions is huge and depends on algorithm, budget and many other factors.

>

logistic.regression =
  function(input, iterations, dims, alpha) {

    lr.map =

      function(., dta) {
        Y = dta[,1]
        X = as.matrix(dta[,-1])
        Z = X %*% t(plane)
        keyval(1, Y * X * g(-Y * as.numeric(Z)))

      }

    lr.reduce =
      function(k, Z)
        keyval(k, t(as.matrix(apply(Z,2,sum))))

    plane = t( rep(0, dims) )

    g = function(z) 1/( 1 + exp(-z) )

    for ( i in 1:iterations ) {
      gradient = values( from.dfs( mapreduce( input, input.format=make.input.format("csv",sep=";"), map = lr.map, reduce = lr.reduce, combine = T ) ) )
      plane = plane + alpha * gradient
    }
    plane
  }
